title: Shopping and comparing
goal: Get by at markets and in shops: ask prices, ask for another size or color, compare two items, and ask people to do things with -아/어 주세요.
bekal: ask a price and understand the answer
ask someone to do something with -아/어 주세요
compare two things with 보다 and 제일

dialogs.title: 대화 — At Namdaemun Market
dialogs.intro: Ani is looking for a jacket. Watch for the pattern -아/어 주세요: it appears four times in this short conversation, and you'll use it every day.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Excuse me, how much is this jacket?

lines.speaker: 주인:
lines.id: That one's forty-five thousand won. It's good quality.
lines.literal: that — forty-thousand — five-thousand — won — is. good-that — item — is.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: It's a bit expensive. Could you give me a discount?

lines.speaker: 주인:
lines.id: Hmm… all right, forty thousand won then.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Thank you! Do you have other colors, though?

lines.speaker: 주인:
lines.id: There's black and white. Which do you like?
lines.literal: black-color — and — white-color — exist. what — subject — good?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Black is nicer than white. May I try it on?
lines.literal: black-color — subject — white-color — than — good. wear — try — even — OK?

lines.speaker: 주인:
lines.id: Yes, go ahead. How's the size?
lines.literal: yes, wear — try. size — as-for — how (honorific)?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: A bit big. Do you have a smaller one?
lines.literal: a-little — big. more — small-that — item — exists?

lines.speaker: 주인:
lines.id: Just a moment, please. Here you go.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: This one's the best. I'll take this one.
lines.literal: this — subject — most — good. this — give.

notes: **-아/어 주세요 means "please do this for me".** Take the 해요 form of the verb, drop 요, and add 주세요. 깎다 → 깎아 → 깎아 **주세요**. 기다리다 → 기다려 → 기다려 **주세요**. This pattern covers almost every request in Korean, and it's much more polite than the bare command -(으)세요.
**주세요 alone is for things, -아/어 주세요 for actions.** 물 주세요 (water, please) but 기다려 주세요 (please wait). Keeping the two apart is a small step that instantly makes your Korean sound more mature.

**보다 means "than" and comes after the thing being compared to.** 흰색**보다** 좋아요 = better than white. Korean needs no separate word for "more" in comparisons — 보다 is enough, though 더 is often added for emphasis: 흰색보다 **더** 좋아요.
**제일 and 가장 both mean "most".** 제일 is more common in speech, 가장 more written. Both go right before the adjective: 이게 **제일** 좋아요.

**-아/어 봐도 돼요? means "may I try?"** It combines two patterns: -아/어 보다 (try doing) and -아도 되다 (may). No need to take it apart yet; memorize the shop phrases whole: 입어 봐도 돼요? (may I try it on?), 먹어 봐도 돼요? (may I taste it?).

**Haggling in Korea has limits.** At traditional markets like Namdaemun or Dongdaemun, haggling is normal and expected. In regular shops, convenience stores, and malls, the price is the price — haggling there isn't clever, it's embarrassing. 좀 깎아 주세요 is a market phrase, not a mall phrase.
**이게 is 이거 + 이 merged.** 이거**가** is never said; the form used is 이게. Likewise 그게 and 저게. As objects: 이걸 (from 이거를), 그걸, 저걸.

**사만 오천 원 = 45,000 won.** Remember that Korean counts in units of 만 (ten thousand): forty-five thousand isn't "forty-five thousand" but "four 만 five 천". Practice reading prices until it's automatic — it's the skill you'll need first if you actually go to Korea.

grammars.title: -아/어 주세요 — asking politely
body: Take the verb's 해요 form, drop 요, attach 주세요. No new rules.
after: **An even more respectful form: -아/어 주시겠어요?** Literally "would you do it for me?". Use it with strangers in more formal situations, or when your request is a real favor: 도와주시겠어요?
**Add 좀 in front and your request instantly sounds friendlier.** 좀 기다려 주세요 is much softer than 기다려 주세요. Nearly all native speakers slip it in.

grammars.title: Comparisons
body: Three patterns that cover every comparison you need at A1.

head: Pattern
Form
Example
Meaning
rows: coffee is more expensive than tea
this one is the same as that
this one is different from that

after: ⚠️ **The order is the reverse of English.** English: "coffee is more expensive **than tea**". Korean: "coffee **tea-than** expensive" — the thing compared to comes first, the adjective last. If you build it in English order, you'll flip the meaning.
**The standard answer to "which is more…?"** is to repeat your choice: 커피하고 차 중에 뭐가 더 좋아요? → 커피가 더 좋아요. 중에 means "among, between".

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: Could you give me a discount?
Do you have a bigger one?

blocks.title: 그냥 볼게요 — your escape line
items: Korean shop staff will come over and offer help almost immediately. If you just want to browse, the phrase is 그냥 볼게요 ("I'm just looking").
It's polite, standard, and instantly understood. Without it, the only way out is usually to leave the shop.
Could you give me a discount?
Do you have a smaller one?

exercises.prompt: Turn into a request with 주세요.

items: Coffee is more expensive than tea.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: 이거 얼마예요? — 조금 비싸요. — 좀 깎아 주세요. — 다른 색 있어요? — 더 작은 거 있어요? — 이걸로 할게요.
커피가 차보다 비싸요. — 이게 더 좋아요. — 이게 제일 커요. — 검은색이 흰색보다 좋아요. — 이게 덜 매워요.
